- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.18) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >75), model often overshoots in the following 3–5 days; apply a 2–5% downward correction to avoid overreaction.
- If model forecast is >10% above recent 18-day average, check sentiment: if sentiment is positive (≥0.36), consider mean reversion; if negative, maintain caution.
- When sentiment is near zero (0.00–0.18) and forecast is high, model is likely overconfident; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next 3–5 days.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome is consistently below forecast (especially in last 5–7 days), apply a “mean reversion” bias: subtract 1–3% from forecast if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is rising (e.g., 0.27–0.53) and forecast is low, model may be underestimating; increase forecast by 1–3% if recent price is trending up.
- Avoid forecasting spikes if sentiment is flat or negative — model tends to overreact; use sentiment as a “calibration” signal to dampen volatility forecasts.
